problems.prompt: Predict the exact terminal output when the following JavaScript snippet executes. Note the variable declaration used in the loop header.
problems.inputHint: e.g. 10, 20 (enter numbers separated by comma or space)
problems.checkpointHint: Check whether 'let' creates a new binding per iteration or reuses a shared single binding.

steps.explain: The loop declares the iterator variable using 'let'. Because 'let' is block-scoped, a new lexical environment binding for 'i' is created for every loop iteration, capturing the specific value (0 through 4) in each closure.
Executing funcs[0]() yields 0, and funcs[4]() yields 4.

problems.fingerprint: scope_hoisting_loop|let-loop|const funcs = []; for (let i = #; i < #; i++) { funcs.push(() => i); } console.log(funcs[#]()); console.log(funcs[#]());

G3.fingerprint: scope_hoisting_loop|let-loop|const funcs = []; for (let i = #; i < #; i++) { funcs.push(() => i); } console.log(funcs[#]()); console.log(funcs[#]());

problems.prompt: Predict the exact terminal output when the following JavaScript snippet executes. Note the variable declaration used in the loop header.
problems.inputHint: e.g. 10, 20 (enter numbers separated by comma or space)
problems.checkpointHint: Check whether 'var' creates a new binding per iteration or reuses a shared single binding.

steps.explain: The loop declares the iterator variable using 'var'. Because 'var' is function-scoped (or global), only a single binding of 'i' exists. When the loop finishes, 'i' holds the terminal value 5.
Executing funcs[0]() yields 5, and funcs[4]() yields 5.

problems.fingerprint: scope_hoisting_loop|var-loop|const funcs = []; for (var i = #; i < #; i++) { funcs.push(() => i); } console.log(funcs[#]()); console.log(funcs[#]());

problems.context: Call Stack vs Microtasks vs Macrotasks
problems.prompt: Trace the execution of Tasks [A, B, C, D, E] through the Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Task Queue. Predict the exact letter sequence printed to the console.
problems.inputHint: e.g. A, B, C, D, E (enter letters separated by comma or space)
problems.checkpointHint: Determine which tasks run synchronously on the Call Stack, then drain Microtasks (C, D) before Macrotasks (B).

steps.explain: Top-level statements execute first synchronously on the Call Stack: Task A logs immediately, Task B (setTimeout) is queued to the Task Queue, Task C (Promise.then) is queued to the Microtask Queue, Task D (queueMicrotask) is queued to the Microtask Queue, and Task E logs synchronously on the Call Stack.
Once the Call Stack empties, the JavaScript engine drains the Microtask Queue completely before picking any Macrotask: Task C (Promise) logs, followed by Task D (queueMicrotask).
Only after the Microtask Queue is completely drained does the event loop execute the next Macrotask: Task B (setTimeout callback) runs and logs.

problems.fingerprint: event_loop_concurrency|direct|// Task A: Synchronous log console.log('A'); // Task B: Macrotask (setTimeout #ms) setTimeout(() => { console.log('B'); }, #); // Task C: Microtask (Promise) Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('C'); }); // Task D: Microtask (queueMicrotask) queueMicrotask(() => { console.log('D'); }); // Task E: Synchronous log console.log('E');

G3.fingerprint: event_loop_concurrency|direct|// Task A: Synchronous log console.log('A'); // Task B: Macrotask (setTimeout #ms) setTimeout(() => { console.log('B'); }, #); // Task C: Microtask (Promise) Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('C'); }); // Task D: Microtask (queueMicrotask) queueMicrotask(() => { console.log('D'); }); // Task E: Synchronous log console.log('E');

problems.prompt: Analyze the asynchronous execution flow below. Predict the single integer printed to the terminal.
problems.checkpointHint: Check whether the async function throws or returns, and whether .catch handles it.

steps.explain: Because input 25 >= 20, compute succeeds and returns resolved Promise(50).
The .catch() is skipped because the Promise resolved. The .then() handler receives 50 and logs 50 + 1 = 51.

problems.context: Prototype Mutation vs Own Property Shadowing
problems.prompt: Analyze the prototype relationship created via Object.create. Predict the three outputs printed to the console in order.
problems.inputHint: e.g. 5, 1, 50 (enter the 3 printed numbers separated by comma or space)
problems.checkpointHint: Differentiate between assigning a new property on child vs mutating an object referenced on proto.

steps.explain: Direct assignment 'child.config = 500' creates an own property on 'child'. It shadows the prototype property without modifying 'proto.config', so proto.config remains 20.

Because 'child' does not have its own 'tags' property, the lookup traverses the prototype chain to 'proto.tags'. Calling .push('itemC') mutates the single shared array on the prototype, increasing proto.tags.length to 2.
Reading child.config retrieves its own shadowed property, evaluating to 500.

problems.fingerprint: prototype_chain_mutation|direct|const proto = { config: #, tags: ['init'] }; const child = Object.create(proto); child.config = #; child.tags.push('itemC'); console.log(proto.config); console.log(proto.tags.length); console.log(child.config);

G3.fingerprint: prototype_chain_mutation|direct|const proto = { config: #, tags: ['init'] }; const child = Object.create(proto); child.config = #; child.tags.push('itemC'); console.log(proto.config); console.log(proto.tags.length); console.log(child.config);

problems.prompt: The following JavaScript code snippet throws a TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') when executed in strict mode. Identify the line number where the reference is extracted without its receiver context.

answerSpec.flawExplanation: Line 11 assigns the method reference directly to 'execute' without preserving its context ('s'). When invoked at line 12 as execute(), 'this' is undefined in strict mode.

problems.inputHint: e.g. 4 (click on the line above or enter line number)
problems.checkpointHint: Trace the method invocation and execution context step-by-step to verify whether the receiver object remains bound at runtime.

steps.explain: At line 11, 'const execute = s.getDetails' strips the receiver ('s') from the function reference. In JavaScript, class methods operate in strict mode by default.
When execute() is invoked as a plain function call without a dot notation receiver, 'this' defaults to undefined, causing property access 'this.name' on line 7 to crash.
To fix this defect, explicitly bind the receiver: 's.getDetails.bind(s)' or wrap in an arrow function: '() => s.getDetails()'.

problems.fingerprint: find_bug_this_binding|direct|class Service { constructor(name, role) { this.name = name; this.role = role; } getDetails() { return `${this.name} (${this.role})`; } } const s = new Service('Charlie', 'Architect'); const execute = s.getDetails; console.log(execute());

G3.fingerprint: find_bug_this_binding|direct|class Service { constructor(name, role) { this.name = name; this.role = role; } getDetails() { return `${this.name} (${this.role})`; } } const s = new Service('Charlie', 'Architect'); const execute = s.getDetails; console.log(execute());
